messages:
Jordan: Quick follow-up after the RFC: I'm proposing we split 'egress binding' responsibilities between control plane and the agent layer. Link to RFC: https://redwood.internal/rfcs/egress-binding-refactor :eyes:
Alex C: Can you summarize the two concrete options again? I skimmed the doc but want the tl;dr for the call later.
Jordan: tl;dr — Option A: control plane maintains global egress policy + allocation table; agent only enforces local NAT/route. Option B: control plane delegates allocation to agents, agents reconcile and report back.
Maria G: Main tradeoffs I see: A = strong central consistency, easier to reason about quotas/overlap. B = better scale/less cp churn but harder to guarantee no CIDR collisions across customers.
Samir: Also consider failure modes: if control plane loses connectivity in A, all new egress mappings stall. In B, agents can continue to allocate (optimistic) but we need conflict resolution.
Jordan: Right. For production, latency-sensitive provisioning pushes me to prefer A for Hosted and Dedicated, but B might be nicer for Private (air-gapped/on-prem) customers.
Emily: One interface question: what does the control->agent API look like? Should be idempotent and cheap to poll. Something like: POST /v1/egress-allocations {customer_id, requested_bindings} and GET /v1/egress-allocations?customer_id
Alex C: I'd prefer a push model with a compact version token so agent can resume: POST + long-poll for delta; avoids constant polling. Keep payloads small (only diffs).
Samir: We need to pin the CIDR range per-customer or per-tenant-subnet? If we pin whole /28 per tenant we waste IPs at scale. Maybe hierarchical: per-tenant small pool, with ephemeral ports mapping on agent.
Maria G: Operationally, auditing and KMS/HSM secrets access require the control plane to be authoritative for Private deployment customers. Can't have agents silently selecting egress addresses there.
Jordan: Good catch; constraints matrix in RFC needs a row for "private/offline deploys" that biases to central allocation.
infra-bot: Deploy check: egress-rfc/2026-03-19 passed CI (unit tests) but integration tests flagged hairpin NAT cases on aws-us-west-2. See job: https://ci.redwood/internal/12345
Emily: For hairpin NAT, agents need to support 1:1 DNAT for internal endpoints. Proposed snippet for agent config: ```yaml
egress:
  mode: delegated # or central
  pool_cidr: "10.50.240.0/28"
  nat_mapping: "ephemeral-ports"
```
Alex C: We should also standardize the status telemetry: allocation_version (int), applied_cidrs (list), last_sync_ts. That helps detect drift during rollouts.
Samir: Conflict resolution idea for B: optimistic allocation + central reconciliation with vector clocks; if conflict detected, control plane issues step-down and tells losing agent to remap (graceful). Might be heavy.
Maria G: Vector clocks feel heavy. Maybe use lease tokens with short TTLs and renewals. If cp unreachable, agents can extend leases up to a safety window.
Jordan: Action items: 1) I'll update RFC to prefer Option A for Hosted/Dedicated and Option B for Private with explicit lease rules. 2) Emily + Alex, design compact push API + status schema. 3) Samir, add integration tests for hairpin NAT + lease expiry.
Alex C: :thumbsup: I'll sketch the API after lunch.
Emily: I'll mock the telemetry and wire the long-poll prototype.
Samir: I'll repro the CI hairpin failure and try a minimal fix.
Jordan: Thanks — if no objections by EOD tomorrow I'll mark RFC as accepted and start a small spike.
Maria G: No objections from me. +1 for the hybrid choice.
infra-bot: Reminder: RFC meeting scheduled tomorrow 15:00 PT (calendar invite sent).
Jordan: Great, we'll sync then.
